topic: the 2017 Congressional Review Act repeal that let ISPs sell your search history without consent
title: The 2017 Law That Let Your Provider Sell Your Search History
description: In 2017, Congress voted to kill a federal rule before it ever took effect, a rule that would have required your internet provider to get your permission before selling your browsing and search history. This AI-narrated commentary breaks down what that rule required, how fast it was repealed, and what it means for your privacy today. #history #privacy #internet

hook_candidates.text: In 2017, Congress voted to let your internet provider sell your entire search history without asking you.
Why does your internet bill never mention who else gets to see your search history?
You think a federal law stops your internet provider from selling your search history. That law never even took effect.
One Senate vote in 2017 decided your internet provider would never need your permission to sell your search history.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who insists deleting their search history keeps it private, because they want to prove their provider could still sell it.
contradicted_belief: Most people assume a federal law already stops their internet provider from selling their search history, but that protection never actually took effect.
closing_comment: Wild that the law meant to protect your search history got repealed in 2017 before it ever took effect. Did your provider ever ask your permission for anything like this?

sources.note: Confirms the March 2017 Senate (50-48) and House (215-205) votes repealing the FCC's 2016 opt-in broadband privacy rule.
Confirms the repeal permanently blocks the FCC from issuing a substantially similar privacy rule without new legislation.

beats.text: Law that could've stopped your internet provider from selling your search history, killed in **2017** before it ever took effect.
beats.broll_query: a hand slamming a rubber stamp marked VOID onto a printed government document, dramatic side light

beats.text: The rule would have forced every provider to ask before selling your data.
beats.broll_query: a laptop screen showing a popup asking allow this site to see your browsing history, blue glow

beats.text: It covered browsing history, app usage, and email content, finalized in **late 2016**.
beats.broll_query: three labeled folders marked browsing, apps, email stacked on a wooden desk, overhead light

beats.text: A permission slip nobody ever signed.
beats.broll_query: a blank permission slip paper curling and yellowing with age on a desk, dust in light

beats.text: Congress killed the rule before providers ever had to follow it.
beats.broll_query: the US Capitol dome at dusk with dark storm clouds gathering behind it

beats.text: The Senate voted **50 to 48**, and the House **215 to 205**, both before the rule ever took effect.
beats.broll_query: a hand pressing a red voting button on a wood paneled senate chamber desk, close up

beats.text: Fastest repeal of an unused rule.
beats.broll_query: a small trophy engraved worlds fastest nothing sitting on a dusty shelf, single spotlight

beats.text: That repeal permanently blocks regulators from writing a similar privacy rule again.
beats.broll_query: a heavy iron padlock chained shut over a stack of blank legal paper, dim room

beats.text: Some states have their own ISP privacy laws now, though coverage still varies.
beats.broll_query: a US map glowing green in a few scattered states while the rest stay gray

beats.text: And that's the part your provider hopes you never look up, so here's one
